title: U.S. Open recap Day 7: Coco Gauff toughs it out on day of upsets and dramatic matches
content:
Follow The Athletic’s U.S. Open coverage

Welcome to the U.S. Open briefing, where The Athletic will explain the stories behind the stories on each day of the tournament.

On Day 7, upsets and tussles, a huge deficit in the draws and a college tennis honor.

Coco Gauff has spent the summer playing like someone who has put her “winning ugly” days behind her.

She bangs aces. She cracks forehands. She comes in and finishes points at the net. She runs like a deer.

Mostly. And not Saturday, when she dipped below her level of the past two months and made 28 errors, including six double faults across 19 games, against Cristina Bucşa of Spain. Gauff did still win, of course, 6-3, 6-4.

The truth is every player has to win a bit ugly sometimes. It may be the most valuable skill there is in a sport where playing at one’s peak is very rare. And there was a whole lot of tussle among the top players in the women’s draw Sunday.

2022 U.S. Open champion Iga Świątek needed to come through two tiebreaks to take out Marie Bouzková of the Czech Republic 7-6(3), 7-6(3). Naomi Osaka, the two-time champion and No. 13 seed, and No. 23 seed Elise Mertens produced a thriller on Louis Armstrong Stadium, which Osaka grabbed 6-3, 3-6, 7-5.

“In the third set, I was just being really overly critical,” Osaka said. “And then it, like, got to a point where I was just like: ‘OK, just fight for everything. See if she is going to close it out on her terms.’

“Like, I started pushing a lot, because I wanted to see if she had the guts to hit winners and go for it.”

At the same time as Osaka played, No. 14 seed Iva Jović and No. 17 seed Alex Eala, two rising stars, were lighting up Arthur Ashe Stadium in prime time, with a 7-5, 3-6, 7-5 win for Jović.

A trio of top Americans could have done with some of that tussle.

2025 finalist Amanda Anisimova looked to be climbing back into her duel with No. 24 seed Anastasia Potapova, but stalled out and lost in straight sets, 6-2, 7-5.

Madison Keys was serving at 5-0 in the third set before Zheng Qinwen stormed back for a 1-6, 7-6(3) 7-5 win.

Taylor Fritz frittered away a two-set lead as he landed just 53 percent of his serves and lost in five to Francisco Cerúndolo.

What allowed Gauff to survive? She covers the court better than maybe anyone in the game. Serves and forehands and backhands have to find tiny spots on the surface. Gauff can cut them off.

So too can Learner Tien, the No. 14 seed on the men’s side. He came from two-sets-to-one down against Jakub Menšík, the No. 17 seed from the Czech Republic, by forcing Menšík to come up with incredible shots and coming up with some of his own in a 6-3, 1-6, 6-7(2), 6-3, 6-4 win.

— Matt Futterman

No player has spent more time on court at the U.S. Open than Alexander Zverev.

The No. 1 seed entered Saturday’s third-round matchup against Alejandro Tabilo having already played two five-set matches for a total of nine hours and 26 minutes of play — at that point the seventh-most time spent on court in the men’s singles event.

His match against Tabilo put him in the top spot, at 11 hours and 51 minutes. But he won it straight sets even after facing two set points in the second set, overcoming the Chilean 6-2, 7-6(2), 6-2.

Having spent the most time on court is generally an unenviable position to be in, both for energy conservation purposes and because Zverev has been working in the dark of night in front of scant crowds who haven’t stuck around for the early-morning hours at the U.S. Open. But Zverev prefers to play on Arthur Ashe Stadium above all else, even the option of an earlier start time on another court.

Besides, his long hours of labor are balanced out with what looks like a flimsy draw on paper.

He wouldn’t face anyone seeded higher than No. 21 before the semifinals, and the only player in his half of the draw to make a Grand Slam semifinal is Russia’s Karen Khachanov.

Zverev has played a ton of tennis this year. But he’s in a good position to make a deep run even without his batteries at full charge.

— Ava Wallace

The day full of tight matches and upsets has wrought a splendid slate in the bottom half of the women’s draw. All four fourth-round matches feature at least one Grand Slam champion — there’s Osaka vs. Elena Rybakina, Świątek vs. Zheng Qinwen, Jović vs. Gauff and Mirra Andreeva vs. Potapova.

Gauff and Rybakina are fighting for world No. 1. The latter, who defeated Ukraine’s Yuliia Starodubtseva in straight sets Saturday, is in pole position to take over from Aryna Sabalenka, but must reach the semifinals. If she does not, one of Sabalenka, Gauff and Pegula could claim the top ranking, but only with a title in New York.

The most enticing matchup might be Osaka vs. Rybakina. Osaka feels primed for a truly deep Grand Slam run after a spring and summer well balanced between rest and good results.

That match just barely edges out Zheng vs. Świątek, a rematch of the 2024 Paris Olympics semifinal in which Zheng stunned Świątek at Roland Garros. The slight worry is that Zheng will run out of gas at some point after coming through the qualifying tournament and winning six matches in New York. That’s the most matches she’s played consecutively since … the Paris Olympics in 2024. It might be OK, though: In a news conference Saturday, Zheng said that winning always makes her feel fresh.

— Ava Wallace

🎾 Women’s singles: Aryna Sabalenka (1) vs. Taylor Townsend

11:30 a.m. on ESPN2, ESPN Unlimited

Townsend gets another round on Arthur Ashe Stadium after last year’s stunning win over Andreeva that took her into the fourth round. The 30-year-old American has backed that up this year, saying in an emotional on-court interview that she needed to prove to herself that she could be as good as last year. Now she faces one of the ultimate hard-court tests in women’s tennis: Sabalenka.

🎾 Men’s singles: Tommy Paul (20) vs. Carlos Alcaraz (2)

Not before 2 p.m. ET on ESPN2, ESPN Unlimited

Given Alcaraz’s limited preparation and the way his serve is starting points but rarely ending them, this match might represent Paul’s best chance to get a Grand Slam win over the Spanish defending champion. Aside from a beatdown at last year’s French Open, when Paul was injured, their matches have hewed to a clear pattern: The first set is close and the American might nick it, before Alcaraz revs into gear, the forehand delta between the two players yawns open and Paul gets taken out of the match. Will this one be different?

🎾 Men’s singles: Daniil Medvedev (7) vs. Frances Tiafoe (11)

Not before 3 p.m. ET on ESPN Unlimited

2021 champion Medvedev has quietly rolled through his first three matches after a long stretch of indifferent results at the majors. Barring his first-round five-setter against compatriot Martin Damm, so too has Tiafoe, who has been playing himself into form for longer than Medvedev. He will have the crowd on his side against one of tennis’ great anti-heroes.

🎾 Women’s singles: Jessica Pegula (3) vs. Sorana Cîrstea

After Medvedev vs. Tiafoe on ESPN Unlimited

Aside from a come-from-behind win over Leylah Fernandez in the previous round, Pegula has mostly rolled, too. The 2024 beaten finalist now meets Cîrstea, who has been undoing many of the narratives surrounding how to retire from tennis in her final season on tour. The 36-year-old Romanian, who has been a threat at just about every tournament she has played, has reached a career-high ranking of No. 17.

Tell us what you noticed on the seventh day…
